RFS-09.Taking inventory: Counting the food on hand regularly, which shows how much was really used and exposes loss or over-ordering.
RFS-09.Comparing supplier prices: Getting quotes from several vendors and negotiating, so the restaurant pays the lowest price for the quality it needs.
RFS-09.Raising menu prices: Charging more for dishes so that the same food cost becomes a smaller share of sales. It risks driving some customers away.
RFS-09.Standardized recipes: Tested recipes with exact ingredients, amounts and steps, so every cook makes the dish the same way at the same cost.
RFS-09.Buying in bulk: Ordering larger quantities to get a lower price per unit. It only saves money if the food is used before it spoils.
RFS-09.Stock rotation: Using the oldest stock first, known as first in, first out, so food does not expire on the shelf.
RFS-09.Proper storage: Keeping food at the right temperature, covered and labeled, so it lasts as long as possible before being used.
RFS-09.Preventing theft: Locking storerooms, limiting who has keys and checking stock, so staff or others cannot walk off with food and drink.
RFS-09.Seasonal ingredients: Buying produce when it is in season, when supply is plentiful and prices are lower.
RFS-09.Checking deliveries: Counting and weighing what arrives and comparing it with the order and the invoice, so the restaurant pays only for what it received.
RFS-09.Recipe costing: Adding up the cost of every ingredient in one portion of a dish, so the menu price can be set to hit the target food cost.
RFS-09.Tracking food cost: Calculating food cost percentage regularly, such as every week, so problems are noticed and fixed quickly.
RFS-09.Training staff: Teaching cooks and servers correct portioning, preparation and storage, so that fewer costly mistakes are made.
RFS-09.Cheaper ingredients: Switching to a less expensive ingredient or cut of meat that still gives acceptable quality.
RFS-09.Menu engineering: Studying each item's popularity and profit, then redesigning the menu to steer guests toward dishes that earn the most.
RFS-09.Par levels: Set amounts of each item that should be on hand. Staff order only enough to bring stock back up to that level.
RFS-09.Forecasting demand: Predicting how many guests will come and what they will order, so the kitchen buys and prepares only what it needs.
RFS-09.Limiting the menu: Offering fewer dishes, which means fewer ingredients to stock and less chance that slow-selling items spoil.
RFS-09.Using leftovers: Turning safe unused food and trimmings into other dishes, such as soups, stocks or daily specials, instead of discarding them.
RFS-09.Cross-utilization: Designing the menu so one ingredient appears in several dishes, which means it is used up faster and less of it spoils.
RFS-09.Yield testing: Measuring how much usable food remains after trimming and cooking, to learn the true cost of each usable portion.
RFS-09.Purchase specifications: Written descriptions of exactly what to buy, such as grade, size and packaging, so the restaurant gets consistent products at fair prices.
RFS-09.Controlling comps and employee meals: Setting limits on free food given to guests and staff and recording it, because given-away food still costs money.
RFS-09.Price contracts with suppliers: Agreements that fix the price of key items for a set period, protecting the restaurant from sudden price jumps.

TRV-01.Leisure tourism: Travel for rest, fun and relaxation during free time, such as a family vacation. It is the most common reason people travel.
TRV-01.Business tourism: Travel for work, including sales trips, meetings, conventions and trade shows.
TRV-01.Ecotourism: Responsible travel to natural areas to enjoy wildlife and scenery in ways that protect the environment and benefit local people.
TRV-01.Cultural tourism: Travel to experience a place's history, arts and traditions, such as visiting museums, historic sites and local festivals.
TRV-01.Adventure tourism: Trips built around physical challenge and some risk outdoors, such as rafting, climbing, trekking or scuba diving.
TRV-01.Sports tourism: Travel to watch or take part in a sporting event, such as going to a championship game or running a marathon in another city.
TRV-01.Medical tourism: Traveling to another place for surgery, dental work or other treatment, often because it is cheaper or available sooner.
TRV-01.Culinary tourism: Travel in which a destination's food and drink are a main reason for going, such as food tours and cooking classes.
TRV-01.Religious tourism: Travel for reasons of faith, such as a pilgrimage to a holy site or attending a major religious gathering.
TRV-01.Agritourism: Visiting working farms and ranches for activities such as picking fruit, farm stays and tours, giving farmers extra income.
TRV-01.Educational tourism: Travel whose main purpose is learning, such as study abroad programs, school trips and language courses.
TRV-01.Wellness tourism: Travel to improve health and well-being through spa treatments, yoga retreats and similar activities.
TRV-01.Event tourism: Travel to attend a planned event such as a music festival, a concert or a major celebration.
TRV-01.Beach tourism: Trips to the coast for sun, sand and sea. It is one of the most popular forms of vacation worldwide.
TRV-01.Visiting friends and relatives: Trips made to see family or friends, shortened to VFR. These travelers often stay in homes instead of hotels.
TRV-01.Voluntourism: Combining a trip with unpaid volunteer work at the destination, such as building homes or helping in conservation projects.
TRV-01.Wine tourism: Visiting vineyards and wineries to tour, taste and buy wine. Also called enotourism.
TRV-01.Shopping tourism: Travel in which buying goods is a main purpose, for example a trip to outlet malls or a city famous for fashion.
TRV-01.Gaming tourism: Travel to gamble at casinos, as in trips to Las Vegas or Macau.
TRV-01.Urban tourism: Visiting cities for their attractions, museums, dining, shopping and nightlife, often on short trips called city breaks.
TRV-01.Romance tourism: Trips taken by couples for honeymoons, anniversaries or destination weddings.
TRV-01.Dark tourism: Visiting places linked to death, disaster or tragedy, such as battlefields, memorials and former prisons.
TRV-01.Space tourism: Paying to travel into space for the experience, a very new and very expensive form of travel offered by private companies.
TRV-01.Genealogy tourism: Traveling to the places one's ancestors came from, to trace family history and see where relatives once lived.
TRV-01.Film tourism: Visiting places because they appeared in a movie or television show.
TRV-01.Bleisure: A blend of business and leisure. A traveler adds vacation days to a work trip to enjoy the destination.
TRV-01.Astrotourism: Travel to places with very dark skies to see stars, eclipses, the northern lights and other sights in the night sky.

TRV-02.Travel agency: A retail business whose advisors plan and book trips for travelers and earn commissions from suppliers or fees from clients.
TRV-02.Online travel agency: A website or app, such as Expedia or Booking.com, that sells flights, hotels and cars from many suppliers. Shortened to OTA.
TRV-02.Tour operator: A company that combines transport, lodging, meals and sightseeing into a package tour and sells it at a single price.
TRV-02.Vacation rental platform: A website such as Airbnb or Vrbo that connects owners of homes and apartments with travelers and takes a fee on each booking.
TRV-02.Tour wholesaler: A company that buys rooms, seats and tours in bulk at low prices and resells them to travel agencies instead of directly to the public.
TRV-02.Metasearch engine: A site such as Kayak or Google Flights that compares prices from many sellers and sends the traveler elsewhere to book.
TRV-02.Meeting planner: A professional who organizes meetings and conventions and so chooses and books the hotels, venues and transport for the group.
TRV-02.Global distribution system: A computer network, such as Sabre or Amadeus, that lets travel agents search and book airline, hotel and car inventory. Shortened to GDS.
TRV-02.Travel management company: An agency that handles business travel for companies, booking trips within the firm's travel policy and reporting on the spending.
TRV-02.Destination management company: A local firm with expert knowledge of one place that arranges tours, transport and events there for visiting groups.
TRV-02.Central reservation system: The system a hotel chain uses to manage room rates and availability and take bookings for all its properties in one place.
TRV-02.Consolidator: A company that buys airline tickets in bulk at special low fares and resells them to travel agencies or the public.
TRV-02.Incentive travel company: A firm that designs and runs reward trips that companies give to top-performing employees or dealers.
TRV-02.Receptive operator: A company based at the destination that provides services for arriving tour groups on behalf of tour operators from elsewhere.
TRV-02.Hotel representation company: A firm that markets independent hotels and takes bookings for them, giving them reach they could not afford alone.

TRV-03.Airplane: The fastest way to cover long distances and the main mode for international trips, though it usually costs more than ground travel.
TRV-03.Car: A traveler's own vehicle. It offers the most flexibility and is the most used mode for leisure trips within the United States.
TRV-03.Train: Passenger rail service between cities. It is slower than flying on long routes but roomy and often arrives in the city center.
TRV-03.Bus: A low-cost road vehicle carrying many passengers. A motorcoach is a bus built for longer trips and tours.
TRV-03.Cruise ship: A large passenger ship that is both the transport and the place to stay, with meals and entertainment on board.
TRV-03.Rental car: A vehicle rented by the day or week, often at an airport, giving visitors freedom to drive at their destination.
TRV-03.Taxi: A licensed car with a driver, hired for a single trip and paid for by a metered or fixed fare.
TRV-03.Rideshare: A ride booked through an app such as Uber or Lyft, in which a driver uses a personal car to carry the passenger.
TRV-03.Subway: An urban rail system, often underground, that moves large numbers of people around a city cheaply.
TRV-03.Ferry: A boat that carries passengers, and often their vehicles, across a body of water on a regular schedule.
TRV-03.Bicycle: A cheap, clean way to get around a destination. Many cities offer bike-share programs that visitors can use.
TRV-03.Recreational vehicle: A motorhome or camper with beds and a kitchen, so it serves as both transport and lodging. Shortened to RV.
TRV-03.Walking: Getting around on foot, which costs nothing and is how most visitors explore compact city centers and attractions.
TRV-03.Shuttle: A van or small bus that runs a fixed route, for example between an airport and hotels.
TRV-03.Motorcycle: A two-wheeled motor vehicle, used by some travelers for touring scenic routes.
TRV-03.Limousine: A luxury car with a professional driver, hired for airport transfers, business travel or special occasions.
TRV-03.Scooter: A small two-wheeled vehicle, such as an electric scooter rented by the minute through an app for short trips in a city.
TRV-03.Van: A vehicle larger than a car that carries a small group and their luggage together.
TRV-03.Private jet: A small aircraft chartered or owned by its passengers, flying on their own schedule at a very high cost.
TRV-03.Streetcar: A rail vehicle that runs on tracks along city streets. Also called a tram or trolley.
TRV-03.Helicopter: An aircraft that can take off and land vertically, used for sightseeing tours and quick transfers.
TRV-03.Yacht: A private or chartered pleasure boat, used for sailing vacations and luxury travel.

TRV-04.Social media: Posting photos, videos and stories on platforms such as Instagram and TikTok to inspire people to visit.
TRV-04.Advertising: Paid messages on television, billboards, magazines, radio and websites that promote the destination to a wide audience.
TRV-04.Website: The destination's official site, where visitors can find things to do, places to stay, events and trip-planning tools.
TRV-04.Branding: Giving a place a clear identity through a name, logo and slogan, such as I Love New York, so it stands out from rivals.
TRV-04.Visitor guide: A printed or digital booklet with maps, attractions, lodging and dining listings that helps people plan a visit.
TRV-04.Influencer partnerships: Working with people who have large online followings to visit and share the destination with their audience.
TRV-04.Festivals and events: Hosting events such as festivals, concerts and sports tournaments that give people a reason to visit at a particular time.
TRV-04.Promotional videos: Short films that show the destination's scenery and experiences, shared on YouTube, social media and television.
TRV-04.Visitor center: A staffed office where travelers get maps, advice and brochures in person, encouraging them to do more and stay longer.
TRV-04.Public relations: Earning unpaid coverage in news and travel media, for example through press releases and stories pitched to journalists.
TRV-04.Email marketing: Sending newsletters and offers to people who signed up, keeping the destination in mind until they book.
TRV-04.Travel packages: Bundles and special offers that combine lodging, attractions and sometimes transport at a price that tempts people to book.
TRV-04.Content marketing: Publishing useful articles, blogs and visitor-made photos and stories that attract people who are researching trips.
TRV-04.Trade shows: Travel industry exhibitions where the destination staffs a booth to meet tour operators, travel agents and meeting planners.
TRV-04.Convention sales: Bidding to bring conferences, conventions and large meetings to the destination, which fill many hotel rooms at once.
TRV-04.Search engine marketing: Paying for search ads and improving the website so the destination appears when people search online for trip ideas.
TRV-04.Partnerships: Joining with airlines, tour operators, hotels and travel agencies to promote the destination and sell trips there together.
TRV-04.Celebrity endorsements: Using a famous person as the face of a campaign to attract attention and add appeal.
TRV-04.Mobile app: A phone application with maps, listings, deals and suggested routes that helps visitors plan and get around.
TRV-04.Online travel site listings: Paid ads and featured pages on booking and review sites such as Expedia and Tripadvisor, where travelers are already planning.
TRV-04.Familiarization trips: Free or low-cost visits, called fam trips, hosted for travel agents and travel writers so they will recommend the place.
TRV-04.Co-op advertising: Advertising in which the destination and local businesses share the cost, so each gets more exposure than it could afford alone.
TRV-04.Film promotion: Attracting movie and television productions to shoot on location, then promoting the places seen on screen to fans.
TRV-04.City passes: A single prepaid card that gives entry to several attractions at a discount, encouraging visitors to see more.
TRV-04.Direct mail: Brochures, postcards or guides sent through the mail to the homes of likely visitors.
TRV-04.Contests and sweepstakes: Giveaways, such as a free trip, that create excitement and collect contact details from people interested in visiting.

TRV-05.Recycling: Collecting paper, glass, plastic and metal separately so they can be made into new products instead of going to a landfill.
TRV-05.Towel and linen reuse: Inviting guests to use towels and sheets for more than one night, which saves the water, energy and detergent used in laundry.
TRV-05.Saving energy: Using less electricity and fuel through measures such as LED lighting, smart thermostats and key cards that switch off the power.
TRV-05.Saving water: Cutting water use with low-flow showerheads, faucets and toilets and by reusing water for gardens.
TRV-05.Renewable energy: Power from sources that do not run out and release little pollution, such as solar panels and wind turbines.
TRV-05.Buying local food: Sourcing ingredients from nearby farms and producers, which cuts transport pollution and keeps money in the community.
TRV-05.Reducing single-use plastics: Replacing throwaway items such as straws, bottles and mini toiletry bottles with refillable or reusable versions.
TRV-05.Reducing waste: Creating less trash in the first place, for example by ordering carefully and donating leftover food.
TRV-05.Hiring local workers: Giving jobs to people who live in the area, so tourism income benefits the community that hosts the visitors.
TRV-05.Composting: Turning food scraps and garden waste into soil instead of sending them to a landfill.
TRV-05.Protecting wildlife habitat: Preserving the natural areas, such as forests and reefs, that animals depend on and that visitors come to see.
TRV-05.Promoting public transit: Encouraging visitors to use buses, trains, bikes and walking instead of cars, to cut traffic and pollution.
TRV-05.Supporting local businesses: Buying from and promoting locally owned shops, guides and suppliers, so that more visitor spending stays in the area.
TRV-05.Limiting visitor numbers: Capping how many people may enter a site, using permits or timed tickets, so crowds stay within its carrying capacity.
TRV-05.Carbon offsets: Paying for projects that reduce greenhouse gases, such as planting trees, to balance the emissions a trip or hotel causes.
TRV-05.Green certification: Approval from an independent body, such as LEED (Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design) or Green Key, confirming a building or business meets environmental standards.
TRV-05.Eco-friendly cleaning products: Cleaners that are non-toxic and break down naturally, so they do less harm to staff, guests and waterways.
TRV-05.Going paperless: Replacing printed bills, forms and keys with digital versions, such as emailed receipts and check-in on a phone.
TRV-05.Preserving local culture: Protecting historic sites, traditions and crafts so that tourism respects the community's heritage instead of wearing it away.
TRV-05.Green building design: Constructing buildings that use less energy and water through features such as insulation, natural light and planted roofs.
TRV-05.Electric vehicle charging: Providing charging stations so guests can travel in electric cars, which produce no exhaust fumes.
TRV-05.Visitor education: Teaching tourists how to behave responsibly, for example staying on trails, taking litter home and respecting local customs.
TRV-05.Conservation fees: Charges or taxes paid by visitors that fund the protection and upkeep of the natural and cultural sites they use.
TRV-05.Spreading visitors out: Promoting quieter seasons and lesser-known places, so famous sites are not overwhelmed and more areas share the benefits.
TRV-05.Community involvement: Giving local residents a say in how tourism is planned and a share in its benefits.

TRV-06.Checked baggage fees: A charge for each suitcase placed in the aircraft hold. It is one of the largest sources of extra income for airlines.
TRV-06.Seat selection fees: A charge to pick a particular seat in advance, with higher prices for aisle, window, exit-row and extra-legroom seats.
TRV-06.In-flight food and drinks: Meals, snacks and alcoholic drinks sold to passengers on board instead of being included in the fare.
TRV-06.In-flight Wi-Fi: Internet access during the flight, sold by the hour, the flight or a monthly plan.
TRV-06.Change fees: A charge for switching to a different flight or date, or for canceling a ticket, after it has been bought.
TRV-06.Seat upgrades: Payment to move to a better cabin, such as premium economy, business or first class, often offered close to departure.
TRV-06.Priority boarding: A fee to board the aircraft early, giving first access to overhead bin space.
TRV-06.Carry-on bag fees: A charge by some low-cost airlines for a bag carried into the cabin and placed in the overhead bin.
TRV-06.Lounge access: Paid entry to the airline's airport lounge, by day pass or annual membership, with seating, food and drinks.
TRV-06.Overweight baggage fees: Extra charges for bags heavier or larger than the airline's limits, or for bulky items such as skis and golf clubs.
TRV-06.In-flight entertainment: Charges for movies, television or headphones on flights where they are not provided free.
TRV-06.Pet fees: A charge for bringing a small animal into the cabin in a carrier or shipping a larger one in the hold.
TRV-06.Travel insurance sales: Trip protection offered during booking. The airline earns a commission from the insurance company on each policy sold.
TRV-06.Hotel and car rental commissions: Payments an airline receives when customers book hotels, rental cars or vacation packages through its website.
TRV-06.Booking fees: Charges for buying a ticket in a particular way, such as by phone with an agent instead of online.
TRV-06.Duty-free sales: Tax-free goods such as perfume, alcohol and gifts sold to passengers on international flights.
TRV-06.Comfort items: Blankets, pillows and amenity kits sold on board, mainly by low-cost airlines.
TRV-06.Fast-track security: A fee for using a quicker security or check-in line at the airport, sold by some airlines as an add-on.
TRV-06.Co-branded credit cards: Cards issued with a bank that carry the airline's name. The bank buys frequent flyer miles from the airline to reward cardholders.
TRV-06.Unaccompanied minor fees: A charge for airline staff to supervise a child who is flying without an adult.
TRV-06.Onboard advertising: Money companies pay to place ads in the in-flight magazine, on seatback screens, tray tables or boarding passes.
TRV-06.Subscription programs: Paid memberships that give customers discounted fares or perks for a yearly or monthly fee.

TRV-07.Theme parks: Purpose-built parks with rides, shows and areas designed around stories or characters, such as Disney World.
TRV-07.Museums: Buildings that collect and display objects of art, history or science for the public to see and learn from.
TRV-07.National parks: Large areas of scenic or natural land protected by the government and open to visitors for hiking, camping and sightseeing.
TRV-07.Beaches: Stretches of sand or shore along oceans and lakes, among the most popular natural attractions for vacations.
TRV-07.Historic sites: Places preserved because of what happened there or who built them, such as monuments, battlefields, castles and ruins.
TRV-07.Zoos and aquariums: Facilities that keep land or sea animals for the public to view, and that also work in conservation and education.
TRV-07.Natural landmarks: Striking features made by nature, such as mountains, waterfalls, canyons and caves, that people travel to see.
TRV-07.Water parks: Amusement parks built around water slides, wave pools and lazy rivers.
TRV-07.Casinos: Venues for gambling on slot machines and table games, often joined to hotels, restaurants and shows.
TRV-07.Festivals: Organized celebrations of music, food, culture or a season that draw visitors for a limited time.
TRV-07.Sports venues: Stadiums, arenas and racetracks where fans travel to watch games and races. Some also offer tours.
TRV-07.Shopping districts: Areas with many stores, such as outlet malls or famous shopping streets, that visitors come to for buying and browsing.
TRV-07.Ski resorts: Mountain areas with lifts, groomed slopes and lodging built for skiing and snowboarding.
TRV-07.Theaters: Venues for live plays, musicals, opera and concerts. Districts such as Broadway are attractions in their own right.
TRV-07.Religious sites: Churches, temples, mosques and shrines visited for worship, pilgrimage or their history and architecture.
TRV-07.Botanical gardens: Gardens that grow and label a wide collection of plants for the public to enjoy and learn about.
TRV-07.Wineries: Places where wine is made, which welcome visitors for tours and tastings. Breweries and distilleries do the same.
TRV-07.Famous buildings: Well-known structures such as skyscrapers, towers and bridges that people visit for their design or the view from the top.
TRV-07.Wildlife reserves: Protected lands where animals live in their natural habitat and visitors can watch them, for example on a safari.
TRV-07.Golf courses: Courses that attract players as a reason to travel, especially famous ones and those attached to resorts.
TRV-07.Nightlife: Evening entertainment such as bars, clubs and live music venues, a draw for visitors to many cities.
TRV-07.Food and markets: A place's well-known restaurants, local dishes and street or farmers markets, which many visitors seek out.
TRV-07.Scenic byways: Roads officially recognized and promoted for the views, history or culture along the route.
TRV-07.Factory tours: Visits to a working plant or studio to see how a product, such as chocolate, cars or films, is made.
TRV-07.Hot springs: Pools of naturally heated water from underground where visitors bathe to relax.
TRV-07.Farms: Working farms, orchards and ranches that open to visitors for tours, picking produce and seasonal events.
TRV-07.Cruises and boat tours: Sightseeing trips by water, such as harbor and river cruises, where the ride and the views are the attraction.

TRV-08.Passport: An official booklet issued by a traveler's own government that proves identity and citizenship. It is required to cross most borders.
TRV-08.Visa: Permission from the destination country to enter for a set purpose and length of time. Not every trip requires one.
TRV-08.Boarding pass: The paper or mobile document issued at check-in that lets a passenger through security and onto a specific flight.
TRV-08.Airline ticket: Proof that a traveler has paid for a seat on a flight, today usually an electronic record with a confirmation number.
TRV-08.Photo ID: A government-issued card with the holder's picture, such as a driver's license or national identity card, carried as a second proof of identity and needed for things such as renting a car.
TRV-08.Travel insurance policy: A contract covering costs such as medical care abroad, canceled trips or lost bags. Some countries require proof of it.
TRV-08.Vaccination certificate: An official record that the traveler has had certain vaccines, such as yellow fever, which some countries demand at entry.
TRV-08.Itinerary: A written plan of the trip listing flights, dates, lodging and activities. Border officers may ask to see it.
TRV-08.Hotel confirmation: Proof of a lodging booking, which shows officials where the traveler will stay.
TRV-08.Customs declaration form: A form on which arriving travelers list goods, cash and food they are bringing into a country.
TRV-08.International driving permit: A booklet that translates a home driver's license into several languages, required to drive or rent a car in some countries.
TRV-08.Return ticket: Proof that the traveler has booked a way out of the country, which many countries require to show the visit is temporary.
TRV-08.Birth certificate: An official record of a person's birth, used to apply for a passport and sometimes to prove a child's age or parentage.
TRV-08.Arrival card: A short form some countries ask visitors to complete on landing, giving their details and the purpose and length of the stay.
TRV-08.Tour and rail vouchers: Prepaid documents that the traveler exchanges for services already bought, such as a tour, a rail journey or a cruise.
TRV-08.Electronic travel authorization: An online pre-approval, such as the United States ESTA (Electronic System for Travel Authorization), that travelers who do not need a visa must get before boarding.
TRV-08.Proof of sufficient funds: Evidence such as bank statements showing the traveler can afford the stay, required for many visas.
TRV-08.Consent letter for a minor: A signed letter from a parent or guardian giving permission for a child to travel without one or both parents.
TRV-08.Prescriptions: A doctor's written order or letter for medicines the traveler carries, which shows customs that the drugs are legal and needed.
TRV-08.Trusted traveler card: A card from a program such as Global Entry or NEXUS that gives approved, low-risk travelers faster border clearance.
TRV-08.Letter of invitation: A letter from a host, employer or organizer in the destination country explaining the visit, often needed for a visa.

EVT-01.Wedding: A social event marking a marriage, usually a ceremony followed by a reception. It involves many vendors and a large budget.
EVT-01.Conference: A meeting, often over several days, where people in one field gather for talks, discussions and networking.
EVT-01.Concert: A live music performance for an audience, which needs a stage, sound, lighting, ticketing and crowd management.
EVT-01.Convention: A large gathering of members of an association, industry or fan community, usually held yearly with sessions and exhibits.
EVT-01.Trade show: An exhibition where companies in an industry rent booths to show their products to buyers and the press.
EVT-01.Festival: A public celebration built around a theme such as music, food or culture, often outdoors and lasting one or more days.
EVT-01.Birthday party: A private social gathering to celebrate someone's birthday, ranging from a small home party to a large hired venue.
EVT-01.Graduation: A ceremony or party marking the completion of school or college.
EVT-01.Fundraiser: An event held to raise money for a charity or cause, such as a gala dinner or auction.
EVT-01.Corporate meeting: A gathering a company holds for its own business, such as a sales meeting, staff meeting or planning session.
EVT-01.Sporting event: An organized competition such as a tournament, race or game, which needs facilities, officials and spectator services.
EVT-01.Reunion: A gathering that brings back together people who share a past, such as family members or former classmates.
EVT-01.Anniversary party: A celebration of the yearly return of an important date, such as a couple's wedding or a company's founding.
EVT-01.Baby shower: A party where guests give gifts to parents expecting a baby. A bridal shower does the same for a bride-to-be.
EVT-01.Prom: A formal dance for high school students, usually held near the end of the school year.
EVT-01.Product launch: An event that introduces a new product to customers and the media to build excitement and coverage.
EVT-01.Seminar: A small educational session in which an expert teaches or leads discussion on one topic.
EVT-01.Awards ceremony: An event that honors achievements by presenting prizes, often with a formal dinner.
EVT-01.Holiday party: A seasonal celebration, often hosted by a company for its employees at the end of the year.
EVT-01.Coming-of-age celebration: A party marking a young person's passage toward adulthood, such as a bar or bat mitzvah, quinceanera or sweet sixteen.
EVT-01.Parade: A public procession of floats, bands and marchers along a street, which requires permits and road closures.
EVT-01.Retreat: A gathering held away from the usual workplace so a group can focus on planning, training or team building.
EVT-01.Grand opening: A celebration of the first day of a new business or location, often with a ribbon cutting.
EVT-01.Funeral: A ceremony honoring a person who has died. It is planned on short notice, often with a gathering afterward.
EVT-01.Networking event: An informal gathering where professionals meet to make business contacts, sometimes called a mixer.
EVT-01.Fashion show: An event where models walk a runway to present a designer's clothing to buyers, press and guests.
EVT-01.Political rally: A public gathering to build support for a candidate or cause, with speeches to a crowd.
EVT-01.Press conference: A staged announcement to which journalists are invited so they can hear news and ask questions.
EVT-01.Virtual event: An event held online through a streaming or meeting platform. A hybrid event has both in-person and online audiences.
EVT-01.Incentive trip: A travel reward a company gives to top-performing employees or dealers to motivate them and recognize their results.
EVT-01.Shareholder meeting: A formal meeting, usually annual, where a corporation's owners hear reports and vote on matters such as electing directors.
EVT-01.Art exhibition: A public showing of artworks in a gallery or other space, often opened with a reception.

EVT-02.Venue: The place where the event will be held. It is usually booked first because it sets the date, capacity and much of the cost.
EVT-02.Budget: A plan of expected income and spending that limits every other choice the planner makes.
EVT-02.Date and time: When the event happens, chosen to suit the guests and avoid clashes with holidays or competing events.
EVT-02.Catering: The food and drink for guests, including the menu, the service style and any special dietary needs.
EVT-02.Entertainment: Music, performers or activities, such as a band, DJ or games, that keep guests engaged.
EVT-02.Invitations: Building the guest list, sending invitations and tracking replies so the planner knows how many people to expect.
EVT-02.Decorations: Flowers, lighting, table settings and other visual touches that carry the event's theme and create the atmosphere.
EVT-02.Agenda: The schedule showing what happens and when, so that the staff, vendors and speakers all follow the same plan.
EVT-02.Marketing: Promoting the event through advertising, social media and publicity so that enough people hear about it and attend.
EVT-02.Transportation: How guests get to and from the event, including parking, shuttles and travel for out-of-town attendees.
EVT-02.Speakers: The people who will address the audience, such as a keynote speaker or host, who must be booked and briefed.
EVT-02.Seating: The room layout and who sits where, which affects how many people fit and how well they can see and talk.
EVT-02.Photography: A photographer or videographer hired to record the event for memories, marketing and sponsors.
EVT-02.Staffing: The paid workers and volunteers needed to run the event, such as servers, ushers and check-in staff.
EVT-02.Audiovisual equipment: Sound systems, microphones, projectors, screens and lighting, often shortened to AV, so guests can see and hear.
EVT-02.Registration: The system for signing up or selling tickets to attendees and checking them in when they arrive.
EVT-02.Lodging: Hotel rooms for out-of-town guests, often reserved as a block at a group rate.
EVT-02.Vendors: The outside suppliers hired for the event, each of whom needs a written contract setting out what they will deliver.
EVT-02.Rentals: Rented items the venue does not supply, such as tables, chairs, linens, tents and staging.
EVT-02.Security: Guards and procedures that control entry, manage crowds and keep guests and property safe.
EVT-02.Permits: Official permission from local government for things such as serving alcohol, closing a street or making noise.
EVT-02.Insurance: A policy that protects the organizer from the cost of accidents, injuries, damage or cancellation.
EVT-02.Sponsors: Companies that give money or products in exchange for exposure at the event, helping to cover its costs.
EVT-02.Signage: Signs and banners that direct guests around the venue and display the names of the event and its sponsors.
EVT-02.Setup and cleanup: Arranging the room and equipment before the event and removing everything afterward, within the venue's time limits.
EVT-02.Party favors: Small gifts or bags of items given to guests to take home as a thank-you or reminder of the event.
EVT-02.Contingency plan: A backup plan for what to do if something goes wrong, such as bad weather, a vendor failing to appear or equipment breaking.
EVT-02.Accessibility: Making sure guests with disabilities can take part, with features such as ramps, reserved seating and sign language interpreters.
EVT-02.First aid: Medical supplies and trained people on site to treat injuries or illness until further help arrives.
EVT-02.Restrooms: Enough toilets for the crowd, which at outdoor events usually means renting portable units.
EVT-02.Post-event evaluation: Reviewing the event afterward, using surveys and results, to learn what worked and what to improve next time.

EVT-03.Hotel: Offers ballrooms and meeting rooms with catering, staff and guest rooms under one roof, which suits conferences and weddings.
EVT-03.Convention center: A very large public building designed for conventions and trade shows, with exhibit halls and many meeting rooms.
EVT-03.Stadium or arena: A sports facility with thousands of fixed seats, used for games, concerts and other events with very large crowds.
EVT-03.Banquet hall: A venue built for private functions such as wedding receptions, with a large dining room and often its own kitchen.
EVT-03.Restaurant: A dining business that can host small events in a private room or be booked out entirely, with food and staff already in place.
EVT-03.Park: A public outdoor space suited to picnics, festivals and ceremonies, which usually needs a permit and a plan for bad weather.
EVT-03.Theater: A hall with a stage and fixed rows of seats, suited to performances, presentations and award shows.
EVT-03.Country club: A private club with a golf course, dining rooms and attractive grounds, often rented for weddings and charity events.
EVT-03.Museum: A cultural building that rents its galleries or halls after hours, giving receptions and galas a memorable setting.
EVT-03.Zoo or aquarium: An animal attraction that rents space for parties and corporate events, with the exhibits as built-in entertainment.
EVT-03.University campus: A school or college with lecture halls, auditoriums and gyms that can be rented, often cheaply, for conferences and competitions.
EVT-03.Community center: A public building run for local residents, with affordable multipurpose rooms for meetings, classes and parties.
EVT-03.Place of worship: A church, temple, mosque or synagogue used for religious ceremonies such as weddings and often for gatherings in its hall.
EVT-03.Beach: An outdoor waterfront setting popular for weddings and parties, which needs permits, rented equipment and a weather backup.
EVT-03.Private home: A house or backyard used for small, personal gatherings, with no rental fee but limited space, parking and facilities.
EVT-03.Bar or nightclub: A nightlife venue with a bar, music system and dance floor already in place, suited to parties and social events.
EVT-03.Fairgrounds: A large open site with barns, halls and fields, used for fairs, festivals, expos and outdoor shows.
EVT-03.Amphitheater: An open-air venue with a stage and rising rows of seats or lawn, used for concerts and performances.
EVT-03.Winery: A vineyard property that hosts weddings, tastings and dinners in a scenic rural setting.
EVT-03.Barn: A farm building, often restored, rented for rustic-style weddings and parties.
EVT-03.Rooftop: The open top of a building fitted out as an event space, valued for its views of the skyline.
EVT-03.Historic estate: An old mansion or grand home with gardens, rented for elegant weddings and receptions, often with rules to protect the property.
EVT-03.Office: A company's own workplace, such as a boardroom or conference room, used for internal meetings at little or no cost.
EVT-03.Casino: A gaming resort that also offers ballrooms, showrooms, restaurants and hotel rooms for conventions and entertainment events.
EVT-03.Tent: A temporary covered structure set up on open ground, which creates an event space almost anywhere outdoors.
EVT-03.Cruise ship: A ship or chartered boat on which a wedding, party or meeting takes place on the water.
EVT-03.Retreat center: A quiet property away from the city, such as a camp or lodge, with lodging and meeting space for group getaways.
EVT-03.Warehouse or loft: A large, open industrial space that planners can decorate and arrange however they like.
EVT-03.Online platform: Software such as Zoom that hosts a virtual event, letting people attend from anywhere without a physical venue.

EVT-04.Theater style: Rows of chairs facing the front with no tables. It fits the most seated people into a room and suits speeches and presentations.
EVT-04.Classroom style: Rows of narrow tables with chairs, all facing the front, so attendees can take notes or use laptops during training.
EVT-04.Banquet rounds: Round tables, usually seating eight to ten people each, spread across the room. The standard layout for meals.
EVT-04.U-shape: Tables arranged in the shape of the letter U with chairs around the outside, so everyone can see the presenter and each other.
EVT-04.Boardroom: One large table with chairs all the way around, used for small meetings where everyone takes part in the discussion.
EVT-04.Reception: A mostly standing layout with a few high tables and little seating, which encourages guests to move around and mingle.
EVT-04.Hollow square: Tables arranged in a closed square or rectangle with an empty middle and chairs around the outside, good for group discussion.
EVT-04.Exhibition: A floor plan of booths and display tables with aisles between them, as used at trade shows.
EVT-04.Cabaret: Round tables with the side nearest the stage left empty, so that no guest sits with their back to the speaker.
EVT-04.Pods: Small clusters of tables around the room, each seating a few people, used for workshops with team activities.
EVT-04.Long tables: Rectangular tables joined end to end with guests seated along both sides, giving a shared, family-style feel to a meal.
EVT-04.Circle: Chairs placed in a ring with no tables, putting everyone on equal terms for open discussion.
EVT-04.T-shape: Tables arranged like the letter T, with leaders seated along the top and other guests down the stem.
EVT-04.Semicircle: Chairs arranged in a half circle facing a presenter, which is less formal than straight rows.
EVT-04.Chevron: Rows of chairs or tables angled toward the front in a V pattern, giving better sightlines than straight rows.
EVT-04.Lounge seating: Sofas, armchairs and low tables arranged in casual groups for relaxed conversation.
EVT-04.E-shape: Tables arranged like the letter E, with a head table and three legs running out from it, used for larger meetings and meals.
EVT-04.Theater in the round: Seating placed on all sides of a central stage or speaker, so the audience surrounds the action.

EVT-05.Caterer: A business that prepares, delivers and serves the food and drink for the event.
EVT-05.DJ or band: A disc jockey who plays recorded music, or live musicians, hired to provide the entertainment and keep guests dancing.
EVT-05.Photographer: A professional who takes still pictures of the event for the hosts, the guests or later marketing.
EVT-05.Florist: Designs and supplies the flower arrangements, such as centerpieces, bouquets and stage displays.
EVT-05.Venue: The business that rents out the event space. Its manager or coordinator works with the planner on rooms, timing and rules.
EVT-05.Videographer: Films the event and edits the footage into a finished video.
EVT-05.Baker: Makes the cake and other desserts, such as a decorated wedding cake made to the client's design.
EVT-05.Bartender: Mixes and serves drinks to guests and is responsible for serving alcohol legally and safely.
EVT-05.Decorator: Designs the look of the event and installs items such as draping, backdrops, table settings and balloons.
EVT-05.Speaker: A person paid to address the audience, such as a keynote speaker who sets the theme of a conference.
EVT-05.Rental company: Rents out items that the venue lacks, such as tents, tables, chairs, linens and dance floors.
EVT-05.Audiovisual company: Provides and operates the sound, microphones, projectors and screens. Audiovisual is often shortened to AV.
EVT-05.Security: Guards hired to check entry, manage the crowd and deal with any trouble.
EVT-05.Transportation company: Provides vehicles and drivers, such as shuttle buses, limousines or charter coaches, to move guests.
EVT-05.Event staff: Temporary workers such as servers, ushers and registration helpers, often supplied by a staffing agency.
EVT-05.Officiant: The person who leads a ceremony, such as the minister or celebrant who conducts a wedding.
EVT-05.Emcee: The master of ceremonies, who hosts the program, introduces speakers and keeps the event moving and on time.
EVT-05.Valet parking service: A company whose attendants park guests' cars on arrival and bring them back at the end.
EVT-05.Printer: Produces printed materials such as invitations, programs, name badges, menus and signs.
EVT-05.Hair and makeup artist: Stylists who prepare people for the event, such as a wedding party or performers.
EVT-05.Photo booth company: Rents out a booth or camera station where guests take fun pictures and get prints or digital copies.
EVT-05.Cleaning crew: Workers who keep the venue tidy during the event and clean up once it is over.
EVT-05.Lighting designer: Plans and operates lighting that sets the mood and highlights the stage or decor.
EVT-05.Graphic designer: Creates the event's visual identity, such as the logo, invitations, signs and web pages.
EVT-05.Insurance agent: Sells the planner an event policy covering risks such as injury, property damage or cancellation.
EVT-05.Medical team: Paramedics or first aid providers on standby to treat injuries or illness, expected at large events.
EVT-05.Interpreter: Translates speech into another language or into sign language so that all attendees can follow.
EVT-05.Pyrotechnician: A licensed specialist who sets up and fires fireworks and other special effects safely.
EVT-05.Portable restroom company: Delivers, services and removes temporary toilets for outdoor events without enough permanent facilities.

EVT-06.Bad weather: Rain, storms, heat or snow that can ruin an outdoor event or stop guests arriving. Planners arrange tents or an indoor backup.
EVT-06.Low attendance: Fewer people coming than expected, which cuts ticket income and leaves paid-for food and space unused.
EVT-06.Vendor no-show: A hired supplier, such as the caterer or DJ, failing to arrive or deliver. Contracts and backup contacts reduce the damage.
EVT-06.Medical emergency: A guest or worker being injured or falling seriously ill during the event, which calls for first aid and an emergency plan.
EVT-06.Going over budget: Spending more than planned because of unexpected or underestimated costs. Planners set aside a reserve for this.
EVT-06.Equipment failure: A breakdown of sound, projection or other gear in the middle of the event. Spare equipment and a technician on site help.
EVT-06.Power outage: Loss of electricity, which stops lighting, sound and cooking. Large events arrange backup generators.
EVT-06.Speaker or performer cancellation: A key presenter or entertainer pulling out, sometimes at the last minute, leaving a gap in the program.
EVT-06.Overcrowding: More people in a space than it can safely hold, which creates a danger of crushing and breaks fire codes.
EVT-06.Security threats: Dangers from people, such as violence, theft or uninvited guests, managed with guards and entry checks.
EVT-06.Fire: A blaze from cooking, candles, wiring or fireworks. Venues must keep exits clear and follow fire safety rules.
EVT-06.Food poisoning: Guests becoming ill from unsafe food, or having allergic reactions. Using licensed caterers and labeling allergens lowers the risk.
EVT-06.Transportation delays: Traffic, flight delays or a lack of parking that make guests, speakers or supplies arrive late.
EVT-06.Alcohol-related incidents: Problems caused by drinking, such as intoxicated guests, underage drinking or drunk driving, for which the host can be held liable.
EVT-06.Staff shortage: Too few workers or volunteers turning up, leading to slow service and long lines.
EVT-06.Running behind schedule: Parts of the program starting late or overrunning, which can cut later items short and lead to overtime charges.
EVT-06.Running out of food: Not having enough food or drink for everyone, usually because more guests came than were counted.
EVT-06.Disease outbreak: A widespread illness, such as a pandemic, that leads to restrictions on gatherings or keeps people from attending.
EVT-06.Property damage: Harm to the venue, rented equipment or belongings, which the organizer may have to pay to repair or replace.
EVT-06.Loss of the venue: The venue becoming unavailable, for example through double booking, closure or damage, forcing a move or cancellation.
EVT-06.Lawsuits: Legal claims brought by someone injured or harmed at the event. Insurance, waivers and good contracts limit the exposure.
EVT-06.Negative publicity: Bad press, protests or angry posts online that damage the reputation of the event and its organizers.
EVT-06.Loss of a sponsor: A sponsor withdrawing its money or support, leaving a hole in the budget that must be filled or cut.
EVT-06.Permit problems: Lacking or breaking a required permit, such as for noise or alcohol, which can bring fines or get the event shut down.
EVT-06.Ticketing system failure: A crash or security breach in the registration or ticketing system, blocking sales or check-in or exposing attendees' data.

EVT-07.Attendance: The number of people who actually came, compared with the target. It is the most basic sign of interest in the event.
EVT-07.Ticket sales: The number of tickets or registrations sold, which shows demand and drives much of the event's income.
EVT-07.Profit: The money left after all the event's costs are subtracted from its income. A loss means costs were higher than income.
EVT-07.Attendee satisfaction: How much guests enjoyed and valued the event, usually measured with a survey sent afterward.
EVT-07.Revenue: The total money the event brought in from tickets, sponsors, exhibitors and sales, before costs are taken out.
EVT-07.Staying within budget: Comparing what was actually spent with what was planned. Finishing at or under budget shows good cost control.
EVT-07.Social media engagement: The number of posts, shares, likes and hashtag uses about the event, showing how much attention it earned online.
EVT-07.Return on investment: The gain from the event compared with what it cost, usually given as a percentage. Shortened to ROI.
EVT-07.Funds raised: The total donations collected at a charity event, compared with the fundraising goal.
EVT-07.Media coverage: The amount and tone of news stories about the event, which give it publicity that was not paid for.
EVT-07.Sponsor satisfaction: Whether sponsors and exhibitors felt they got value for their money, often shown by whether they sign up again.
EVT-07.Meeting objectives: Checking results against the specific goals set before the event, such as training staff or launching a product.
EVT-07.Sponsorship revenue: The money companies paid to be associated with the event, an important income source for many events.
EVT-07.Leads generated: The number of potential customers or contacts collected, a key measure for trade shows and business events.
EVT-07.Repeat attendance: The share of attendees who came to a previous edition or say they would come again, a sign of loyalty.
EVT-07.No-show rate: The percentage of people who registered but did not come. A high rate wastes food and seats.
EVT-07.Attendee engagement: How actively people took part, for example by going to sessions, asking questions, voting in polls or using the event app.
EVT-07.Brand awareness: How much more people know about and recognize the host or sponsor's brand as a result of the event.
EVT-07.Website traffic: The number of visits to the event's or host's website before and after, showing the interest the event created.
EVT-07.Cost per attendee: Total spending divided by the number of people who came, which lets planners compare the efficiency of different events.
EVT-07.Net promoter score: A score based on asking attendees how likely they are, from 0 to 10, to recommend the event to others.
EVT-07.Economic impact: The money the event brought into the local area through visitors' spending on hotels, meals, transport and shopping.
EVT-07.Safety record: The number of injuries, accidents and security incidents. Few or none shows that risks were well managed.
EVT-07.Staff and vendor feedback: Comments gathered from workers, volunteers and suppliers in a debrief, revealing what ran smoothly behind the scenes.

EVT-08.Rental fee: The price the planner agrees to pay for the use of the space, the central money term of the contract.
EVT-08.Event date and time: The exact day and hours the space is reserved, including when the planner's access begins and ends.
EVT-08.Deposit: Money paid up front to hold the date. It may be kept by the venue if the planner cancels or the property is damaged.
EVT-08.Cancellation policy: The terms that say what happens if either side cancels, including deadlines and how much money is refunded or owed.
EVT-08.Payment schedule: The dates on which each part of the total is due, such as a deposit at signing and the balance before the event.
EVT-08.Capacity limit: The largest number of people allowed in the space, set by fire and safety codes.
EVT-08.Space and services provided: A description of exactly which rooms, equipment, furniture and staff the venue will supply for the fee.
EVT-08.Names of the parties: Identifies who is entering the agreement, the venue and the client, with the signatures that make it binding.
EVT-08.Insurance requirement: A term requiring the planner to carry liability insurance and give the venue proof of the coverage before the event.
EVT-08.Damage clause: Makes the planner responsible for paying for any harm that guests or vendors cause to the venue's property.
EVT-08.Food and beverage minimum: The least amount the client must spend on catering. If orders fall short, the client pays the difference anyway.
EVT-08.Setup and teardown times: The hours when vendors may enter to set up and the time by which everything must be removed.
EVT-08.Guaranteed guest count: The final number of guests the planner confirms by a deadline. The venue charges for at least that many, even if fewer come.
EVT-08.Force majeure: A clause that excuses both sides from the contract if an event beyond their control, such as a natural disaster, makes it impossible.
EVT-08.Indemnification: A promise by one party to cover the other's losses and legal costs if its actions lead to a claim. Also called hold harmless.
EVT-08.Alcohol policy: Rules on who may serve alcohol, when service ends and who carries the legal responsibility for it.
EVT-08.Rules and restrictions: The venue's limits on matters such as noise, closing time, decorations, candles and smoking.
EVT-08.Service charge and taxes: A fixed percentage the venue adds to food and drink bills, plus sales tax, which can raise the total cost well above the quoted price.
EVT-08.Overtime charges: Extra fees charged if the event runs past the contracted end time.
EVT-08.Cleaning fee: A charge for cleaning the space afterward, or a statement of what cleanup the client must do.
EVT-08.Attrition clause: Sets how far the number of guests or hotel rooms can fall below what was promised before the planner must pay a penalty.
EVT-08.Room block: A set number of hotel rooms held for the event's guests at an agreed rate until a cutoff date.
EVT-08.Vendor restrictions: Terms that limit which outside suppliers may be used, for example requiring the venue's own caterer or approved vendors.
EVT-08.Dispute resolution: States how disagreements will be settled, such as through mediation or arbitration, and which state's law applies.
EVT-08.Security requirement: A term requiring a set number of security guards, often based on guest count or whether alcohol is served.
EVT-08.Rescheduling policy: Explains whether the event can be moved to another date, how much notice is needed and what it costs.

SPE-01.Ticket sales: Money from fans buying admission to games, including single-game and season tickets. Also called gate receipts.
SPE-01.Merchandise: Sales of jerseys, hats and other goods carrying the team's name and logo, in team stores and online.
SPE-01.Concessions: Food and drink sold to fans inside the stadium or arena on game days.
SPE-01.Sponsorships: Fees companies pay to be linked with the team, in return for exposure such as signs, jersey patches and promotions.
SPE-01.Broadcast rights: Fees television, radio and streaming companies pay for the right to show the games. For the biggest leagues this is often the largest income source.
SPE-01.Parking: Fees fans pay to park in lots the team owns or controls on game days.
SPE-01.Luxury suites: Private boxes and premium club seats leased at high prices, mostly to companies that use them to entertain clients.
SPE-01.Advertising: Money from selling ad space on stadium boards, scoreboards, programs and the team's own media.
SPE-01.Naming rights: A fee a company pays, usually over many years, to have its name on the team's stadium or arena.
SPE-01.Licensing: Royalties paid by manufacturers for permission to make and sell products that carry the team's logos.
SPE-01.Revenue sharing: Money the league collects centrally, such as national television income, and divides among all its teams.
SPE-01.Facility rentals: Income from renting the stadium or arena for concerts, other sports and private events on days without games.
SPE-01.Prize money: Payments for winning or advancing in competitions, such as tournament winnings or playoff bonuses.
SPE-01.Digital subscriptions: Fees fans pay for the team's own streaming service, app or other online content.
SPE-01.Camps and clinics: Fees from youth training programs run under the team's name, which also build future fans.
SPE-01.Personal seat licenses: A one-time fee a fan pays for the right to buy season tickets for a specific seat. Shortened to PSL.
SPE-01.Player transfer fees: Money one club pays another to take over a player's contract, a major income source in world soccer.
SPE-01.Stadium tours and fan experiences: Paid behind-the-scenes tours and special access, such as meeting players or going onto the field.
SPE-01.Real estate development: Income from shops, restaurants, hotels and offices the team's owners build and rent out around the stadium.
SPE-01.Fan club memberships: Yearly fees fans pay to join an official club that offers perks such as early ticket access and exclusive gifts.

SPE-02.Signage: The sponsor's name and logo shown on boards, banners and screens around the venue, where fans and cameras see them.
SPE-02.Naming rights: The right to put the company's name on the stadium, arena or another part of the venue.
SPE-02.Jersey patch: The sponsor's logo sewn or printed on players' uniforms, where it is seen in every game and photo.
SPE-02.Free tickets: A set number of seats included in the deal, which the sponsor uses for clients, employees and contests.
SPE-02.Hospitality: Use of a suite or VIP area with food and drink, where the sponsor entertains important customers.
SPE-02.Use of team logos: Permission to put the team's or event's name and marks in the sponsor's own advertising and packaging.
SPE-02.Social media mentions: Posts on the team's official accounts that feature or thank the sponsor, reaching the team's followers.
SPE-02.Official sponsor designation: The right to call itself the official product or partner of the team, such as the official airline.
SPE-02.Public address announcements: The sponsor's name or message read aloud over the venue's loudspeakers during the game.
SPE-02.Player appearances: Visits by athletes to the sponsor's stores or events, to meet customers and draw a crowd.
SPE-02.Program advertising: An ad for the sponsor printed in the game or event program that fans read.
SPE-02.Broadcast commercials: Advertising time during the radio or television coverage of the games, included in the package.
SPE-02.Category exclusivity: A promise that no competitor in the same product category, such as another soft drink, may sponsor the same property.
SPE-02.On-site activation: The right to set up a booth or display at the venue to hand out samples, show products and meet fans in person.
SPE-02.Title sponsorship: The top level of sponsorship, in which the company's name becomes part of the event's name. A presenting sponsor, one step below, is credited with the words presented by.
SPE-02.Website and digital ads: The sponsor's logo and ads placed on the team's website, app and emails to fans.
SPE-02.Sponsored promotions: A giveaway or theme night carrying the sponsor's name, such as a free item given to fans with its logo on it.
SPE-02.In-game features: Regular segments during the game presented under the sponsor's name, such as a replay, a contest or the kiss cam.
SPE-02.VIP experiences: Special access that fans cannot buy, such as going onto the field before the game or touring the locker room.
SPE-02.Press backdrop: The sponsor's logo printed on the wall behind players and coaches at interviews, so it shows in media coverage.
SPE-02.Parking passes: Reserved parking spaces close to the venue for the sponsor's guests.
SPE-02.Pouring rights: The exclusive right for a beverage company to have its drinks sold throughout the venue.
SPE-02.Access to fan data: Permission to send offers to the team's fan contact list, within privacy rules, to reach likely customers.
SPE-02.Community program tie-ins: The sponsor's name attached to the team's charity or youth programs, linking the company to a good cause.
SPE-02.Right of first refusal: The sponsor's right to renew or match any rival offer before the team can sell the sponsorship to another company.
SPE-02.Co-branded merchandise: Products or giveaway items that carry both the team's and the sponsor's logos.

SPE-03.Single-game ticket: Admission to one game or event, bought on its own. It suits casual fans who attend only now and then.
SPE-03.Season ticket: A package covering every home game of the season in the same seat, giving the team guaranteed income before play begins.
SPE-03.General admission: Entry without an assigned seat. Fans sit or stand wherever there is room in the area, first come, first served.
SPE-03.Group tickets: A block of seats sold together at a discount to a group, such as a company, school or youth team.
SPE-03.VIP ticket: A higher-priced ticket that adds extras such as the best seats, a private entrance, a lounge or a chance to meet the performers.
SPE-03.Partial season plan: A package of selected games, such as half the season or all weekend games, for fans who cannot commit to every game.
SPE-03.Luxury suite: A private enclosed room overlooking the action, with its own seating and catering, rented for a game or leased for a season.
SPE-03.Student ticket: A discounted ticket for students with valid identification, often in a special student section.
SPE-03.Reserved seat: A ticket for one specific, numbered seat that is held for that buyer.
SPE-03.Family pack: A bundle of several tickets, often with food or drinks included, sold at one reduced price to attract families.
SPE-03.Standing room only: A cheaper ticket with no seat. The holder watches from a marked standing area, usually once the seats have sold out.
SPE-03.Club seat: A premium seat with extras such as wider chairs, access to an indoor lounge and better food service.
SPE-03.Courtside seats: The seats closest to the action, right beside the court or field, and among the most expensive in the building.
SPE-03.Discounted child or senior ticket: A reduced price offered to certain age groups, such as children and older fans, to make attending more affordable.
SPE-03.Day or multi-day pass: Admission to everything happening on one day, or over several days, of a festival or tournament.
SPE-03.Presale ticket: A ticket sold before the general public sale, often to fan club members or cardholders, sometimes at a lower price.
SPE-03.Flex plan: A bundle of vouchers that the fan exchanges for tickets to whichever games they choose.
SPE-03.Playoff tickets: Tickets to postseason games, usually sold at higher prices and offered first to season ticket holders.
SPE-03.All-inclusive ticket: A ticket whose price includes unlimited or set amounts of food and drinks as well as the seat.
SPE-03.Resale ticket: A ticket sold again by its first buyer on a secondary market such as StubHub, at a price set by demand.
SPE-03.Parking pass: A prepaid permit to park at the venue, sold alongside tickets or bundled into packages.
SPE-03.Ticket and merchandise bundle: A package that pairs a ticket with an item such as a hat or shirt, often for a theme night.
SPE-03.Subscription pass: A monthly fee that lets a fan attend many or all games in that month, often standing or in whatever seats are free.
SPE-03.Complimentary ticket: A free ticket, called a comp, given to sponsors, players' families, charities or guests of the team.
SPE-03.Accessible seating: Spaces for fans who use wheelchairs or have other disabilities, sold with nearby seats for their companions.
SPE-03.Obstructed-view ticket: A cheaper ticket for a seat where a pole, railing or other object blocks part of the view.

SPE-04.Jerseys: Copies of the shirts players wear, often with a star's name and number. They are among the best-selling team products.
SPE-04.Hats: Caps, beanies and other headwear with the team or brand logo, a low-priced item many fans buy.
SPE-04.T-shirts: Casual shirts printed with logos, slogans or characters. They are cheap to make and sell in very large numbers.
SPE-04.Hoodies: Sweatshirts, jackets and other warm outerwear carrying the brand's name or logo.
SPE-04.Toys: Playthings such as action figures, plush animals, bobbleheads and board games based on characters or teams.
SPE-04.Video games: Games that use real teams, players or characters under license, such as official league sports titles.
SPE-04.Trading cards: Collectible cards picturing players or characters, sold in packs and traded among fans.
SPE-04.Posters: Printed pictures, wall art and calendars showing players, teams or scenes from films.
SPE-04.Drinkware: Mugs, cups, tumblers and water bottles decorated with the brand's logo.
SPE-04.Apparel accessories: Small clothing extras such as socks, scarves, gloves, ties and sunglasses carrying the logo.
SPE-04.Footwear: Shoes, sneakers, slippers and sandals in team colors or with licensed designs.
SPE-04.Collectibles: Items bought to keep and display, such as autographed balls, memorabilia used in games and limited-edition figures.
SPE-04.Flags and banners: Flags, pennants and banners that fans hang at home, in the yard or on the car to show support.
SPE-04.Bags: Backpacks, tote bags, lunch boxes and wallets printed with logos or characters.
SPE-04.Sporting goods: Balls, mini helmets and other sports equipment decorated with team logos.
SPE-04.Keychains and pins: Small, cheap souvenirs such as keychains, lapel pins, magnets and stickers, often bought on impulse.
SPE-04.Home goods: Household items such as blankets, bedding, towels and kitchenware carrying the brand.
SPE-04.Jewelry: Watches, necklaces, rings and bracelets featuring a team's or brand's logo.
SPE-04.Phone cases: Protective covers and other tech accessories decorated with logos or characters.
SPE-04.School and office supplies: Notebooks, folders, pens and similar stationery printed with characters or team logos.
SPE-04.Food and beverages: Packaged snacks, cereal, candy and drinks sold with a team, film or character on the label.
SPE-04.Books and media: Books, magazines, comics, DVDs and soundtracks based on the team or entertainment property.
SPE-04.Baby and kids apparel: Clothing in children's sizes, such as infant bodysuits and small jerseys, bought by fans for their families.
SPE-04.Pet products: Items for animals, such as dog jerseys, collars, leashes and toys with team logos.
SPE-04.Auto accessories: Products for cars, such as license plate frames, decals, car flags and seat covers.
SPE-04.Tailgating gear: Equipment for parties in the parking lot before a game, such as coolers, grills, folding chairs and tents with the team logo.
SPE-04.Costumes: Dress-up outfits that let fans look like a film or cartoon character, sold especially for Halloween.
SPE-04.Health and beauty products: Personal care items such as cosmetics, fragrances and soaps sold under a team's or entertainment brand's name.

SPE-05.Giveaways: Free items, such as bobbleheads, shirts or hats, handed to fans at the gate, often only to the first several thousand to arrive.
SPE-05.Discounted tickets: Lower prices or deals such as two tickets for the price of one, used to fill seats at games that would sell poorly.
SPE-05.Theme nights: Games built around a theme, such as a popular movie or a college night, with matching music, decorations and special items.
SPE-05.Fireworks: A fireworks show after the game, a classic way of drawing families, especially on summer weekends.
SPE-05.Advertising: Paid messages on television, radio, billboards and online that tell the public about upcoming games and offers.
SPE-05.Food and drink specials: Reduced prices on concession items, such as dollar hot dog night, that make a game cheaper to attend.
SPE-05.Fan appreciation night: A game, often near the end of the season, when the team thanks its fans with prizes, discounts and giveaways.
SPE-05.Halftime shows: Entertainment during the break in play, such as bands, performers or acrobats, that adds value beyond the game itself.
SPE-05.Contests and sweepstakes: Chances for fans to win prizes, such as raffles, drawings or a contest on the field during a break.
SPE-05.Postgame concerts: A live music act that performs after the game and is included in the ticket price, attracting fans of the artist.
SPE-05.Autograph sessions: Set times when fans can meet players, get autographs and take photos with them.
SPE-05.Social media campaigns: Posts, hashtags and online contests that build excitement for coming games and reach younger fans.
SPE-05.In-game entertainment: Activities during breaks in play, such as mascot races, the kiss cam and T-shirt tosses, that keep the crowd having fun.
SPE-05.Family packs: Bundles of tickets with food and drinks at one low price, making a game affordable for parents with children.
SPE-05.Group outings: Discounted blocks of tickets, with extras such as a scoreboard welcome, sold to companies, schools and scout troops.
SPE-05.Heritage nights: Games that celebrate a particular culture or community with music, food and special merchandise, drawing new groups of fans.
SPE-05.Kids days: Games with activities for children, such as running the bases afterward or free meals for kids.
SPE-05.Military and first responder nights: Games honoring service members, veterans, police, firefighters and similar groups, usually with free or discounted tickets for them.
SPE-05.Celebrity appearances: A famous guest or former star player who attends, for example to throw the first pitch or sign autographs.
SPE-05.Mascot appearances: The team's costumed character visiting schools and community events and greeting fans at games, which appeals to children.
SPE-05.Ticket bundles: Packages that combine tickets to several games, or a ticket with food or merchandise, at a better overall price.
SPE-05.Email and text offers: Special deals sent directly to fans on the team's contact list, often for games coming up soon that have seats left.
SPE-05.Loyalty rewards program: A program in which fans earn points for attending and buying, then trade them for prizes and experiences.
SPE-05.Throwback nights: Games where the team wears old-style uniforms and celebrates its history, appealing to fans' nostalgia.
SPE-05.Dog nights: Games where fans may bring their dogs, usually into a special section, often called bark in the park.
SPE-05.Charity nights: Games tied to a good cause, with part of the ticket price or the proceeds of an auction donated to a charity.

SPE-06.Cartoon characters: Fictional characters such as Mickey Mouse or superheroes, whose images are licensed for toys, clothing and countless other products.
SPE-06.Movies and TV shows: Film and television titles, such as Star Wars, whose names, logos and scenes are licensed to product makers.
SPE-06.Sports teams: Professional teams and leagues, which license their names, logos and colors for clothing and fan gear.
SPE-06.Celebrities: Famous people who let companies use their name or face on products in exchange for payment.
SPE-06.Athletes: Individual sports stars, who license their name, image and likeness for items such as shoes, jerseys and video games.
SPE-06.Corporate brands: Well-known company trademarks, such as Coca-Cola, licensed for products outside the company's own line, like clothing or toys.
SPE-06.Colleges: Universities, which license their names, logos and mascots for clothing and gifts sold to students, alumni and fans.
SPE-06.Music artists: Singers and bands, whose names, logos and album artwork are licensed for shirts, posters and other merchandise.
SPE-06.Video games: Game titles and their characters, such as Mario or Pokemon, licensed for toys, clothing and films.
SPE-06.Books: Novels, comics and children's books whose characters and titles are licensed for films, toys and other goods.
SPE-06.Fashion designers: Designer names licensed to other manufacturers for products such as perfume, eyewear and watches.
SPE-06.Toy brands: Toy names such as Lego or Barbie that are licensed for other products, including films, clothing and video games.
SPE-06.Artwork: Paintings, illustrations and photographs licensed by artists or museums for prints, stationery and home decor.
SPE-06.Nonprofit organizations: Charities that license their name and logo to companies, raising money and awareness through the products sold.
SPE-06.Major events: Large events such as the Olympics or the World Cup, which license their names and emblems for official souvenirs.
SPE-06.Broadway shows: Stage musicals and plays, which license their titles and artwork for souvenirs, recordings and clothing.
SPE-06.Military branches: Armed services such as the U.S. Army and Navy, which own trademarks on their names and emblems and license them for goods.
SPE-06.Historical figures: Famous people who have died, whose estates may still control and license the use of their name and image.
SPE-06.Greek organizations: College fraternities and sororities, which license their letters and crests for clothing and gifts.
SPE-06.Places and landmarks: Cities, parks and famous sites whose protected names, logos or slogans are licensed for souvenirs.

SPE-07.Coach: Trains the athletes, plans strategy and makes decisions during games. Assistant coaches handle particular areas such as strength training.
SPE-07.Sports agent: Represents athletes in contract talks with teams and sponsors and is paid a percentage of the deals.
SPE-07.General manager or team president: The general manager builds the roster through signings and trades. The president runs the business side of the club.
SPE-07.Broadcaster or journalist: Describes games on television or radio, or reports on teams and players for news outlets.
SPE-07.Athletic trainer: A health care professional who works to prevent injuries, treats them when they happen and guides players' recovery.
SPE-07.Referee: An official who enforces the rules during a game and settles disputes. Called an umpire in some sports.
SPE-07.Scout: Travels to watch and evaluate players so the team knows whom to draft, sign or trade for.
SPE-07.Marketing director: Plans how the team is promoted to fans, including advertising, promotions and the image of the brand.
SPE-07.Ticket sales representative: Sells season tickets, group packages and single-game tickets, often by phoning fans and local businesses.
SPE-07.Public relations director: Manages the team's relationship with the media, writing press releases and arranging interviews.
SPE-07.Event coordinator: Organizes what happens on game day and at other events, from scheduling to staff and entertainment.
SPE-07.Facility manager: Runs the stadium or arena, overseeing maintenance, safety, cleaning and preparation for each event.
SPE-07.Team owner: The person or group that owns the franchise, pays for it and makes the final decisions about the business.
SPE-07.Athletic director: Heads a school's or college's sports department, hiring coaches and managing budgets and facilities.
SPE-07.Team physician: A medical doctor who diagnoses and treats players' injuries and decides when they are fit to play.
SPE-07.Social media manager: Creates and posts content on the team's online accounts and interacts with fans there.
SPE-07.Event promoter: Organizes, finances and markets sporting events such as boxing matches, and earns money from their ticket and media sales.
SPE-07.Sponsorship sales manager: Sells sponsorship packages to companies and makes sure sponsors receive everything they were promised.
SPE-07.Sports psychologist: Helps athletes with the mental side of performance, such as focus, confidence and coping with pressure.
SPE-07.Nutritionist: Plans what athletes eat and drink so they have the energy to perform and recover well.
SPE-07.Equipment manager: Orders, fits, maintains and transports the team's uniforms and gear.
SPE-07.Sports photographer: Takes pictures or video of games and players for the team, the media or sponsors.
SPE-07.Sports lawyer: Handles legal matters such as player contracts, sponsorship agreements and disputes.
SPE-07.Game day staff: Part-time workers who serve fans at events, including ushers, ticket takers, security guards and concession workers.
SPE-07.Cheerleader: Performs routines at games to entertain the crowd and build support for the team.
SPE-07.Groundskeeper: Looks after the playing surface, such as the grass, dirt or turf, so that it is safe and ready for play.
SPE-07.Statistician: Records and analyzes game and player data. Teams use the findings to judge players and plan strategy.
SPE-07.Mascot: A performer who wears the team's character costume to entertain fans at games and community events.
SPE-07.Merchandise manager: Runs the team's stores and product sales, choosing what items to stock and how to price them.
SPE-07.Community relations director: Organizes the team's charity work, player visits and youth programs to build goodwill in the local area.
SPE-07.Team accountant: Tracks the club's income, spending and payroll and prepares its financial reports.
SPE-07.Team travel coordinator: Arranges the flights, buses, hotels and meals the team needs for away games.

SPE-08.Salary: The fixed pay a team gives a player under a contract for a season or a number of years.
SPE-08.Endorsements: Payments from companies to a star who publicly backs their products, for example by appearing in ads or wearing the brand.
SPE-08.Prize money: Money awarded for winning or placing well in a competition. In individual sports such as golf and tennis it takes the place of a team salary.
SPE-08.Bonuses: Extra payments written into a contract, such as a signing bonus or rewards for reaching performance targets.
SPE-08.Social media content: Income from sponsored posts, ad revenue and paid partnerships on platforms such as YouTube, Instagram and TikTok.
SPE-08.Appearance fees: Payment simply for showing up, for example at a tournament, a store opening or a corporate event.
SPE-08.Merchandise sales: A share of the money from products that carry the star's name, such as an entertainer's tour shirts.
SPE-08.Concert and tour ticket sales: The performer's share of ticket revenue from live shows. For many musicians it is the largest source of income.
SPE-08.Royalties: Payments made each time a creative work is sold, streamed or broadcast, such as a song or a rerun of a television show.
SPE-08.Own business ventures: Profits from companies the star starts or owns, such as a clothing line, a restaurant or a production company.
SPE-08.Licensing their name and likeness: Fees for permission to use the star's name or image, for example in a video game or on trading cards.
SPE-08.Acting and media work: Pay for roles in films and television, hosting shows, podcasts or working as a commentator.
SPE-08.Speaking engagements: Fees for giving talks to companies, schools and conferences, often about motivation or their career.
SPE-08.Autograph signings: Payment for signing items at shows and events, or for signing memorabilia that dealers then sell.
SPE-08.Camps and clinics: Fees from training camps and lessons run under the star's name for young athletes or students.
SPE-08.Book deals: An advance and royalties from a publisher for a memoir or other book, often written with a professional writer.
SPE-08.Investments: Returns from putting money into stocks, property or shares of companies, sometimes taken in place of cash from a sponsor.
SPE-08.Personalized video messages: Fees fans pay for a short custom video greeting from the star, through services such as Cameo.
SPE-08.Pension and deferred pay: Money paid out later. Leagues fund retirement plans for players, and some contracts delay part of the salary for years.

SPE-09.Box office: Money from tickets sold at movie theaters. The studio and the theater owner each keep a share of every ticket.
SPE-09.Streaming rights: Fees a streaming service pays to carry the film, or the value it brings to the studio's own service by attracting subscribers.
SPE-09.Merchandise: Royalties from toys, clothing and other products based on the film. For some franchises this earns more than ticket sales.
SPE-09.DVD and Blu-ray sales: Sales of physical discs for watching at home, once a huge source of income and now much smaller.
SPE-09.Digital rentals and purchases: Fees viewers pay to rent or buy the film online, known as video on demand.
SPE-09.Television rights: Fees paid by broadcast and cable networks for the right to show the film on their channels.
SPE-09.International distribution: Income from releasing the film in other countries, through the studio's own offices or by selling rights to local distributors.
SPE-09.Product placement: Fees brands pay to have their products shown or used on screen within the film.
SPE-09.Soundtrack sales: Income from sales, streams and licensing of the film's songs and score.
SPE-09.Promotional tie-ins: Deals with partners such as fast food chains that pay to link their products to the film and help advertise it.
SPE-09.Video game adaptations: Fees and royalties from game makers licensed to create games based on the film.
SPE-09.Sequels and spin-offs: Further films and series built on a successful original, which earn new income from the same characters and world.
SPE-09.Theatrical re-releases: Bringing an older film back to theaters, often for an anniversary or in a new format, to sell tickets again.
SPE-09.Theme park attractions: Rides and themed areas based on the film, either in the studio's own parks or licensed to other park operators.
SPE-09.Airline and hotel licensing: Fees for showing the film outside theaters and homes, such as on flights, on cruise ships and in hotel rooms.
SPE-09.Book and comic tie-ins: Royalties from novelizations, comics and art books that publishers produce under license from the studio.
SPE-09.Stage adaptations: Income from turning the film into a live stage show, such as a Broadway musical.
